title: Paths to Democracy: Exploring Regime Transitions and Democratic Stability in the Commonwealth of Nations
text:
5.1 Commonwealth Background

Codeworld <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf")

commonwealth_1950 <- commonwealth |>
  filter(year == 1950)

world <- world |>
  mutate(is_commonwealth = name %in% commonwealth_1950$country_name)

ggplot(data = world) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = is_commonwealth), color = "blue") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "red", "FALSE" = "grey90")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Commonwealth Countries in 1950", fill = "Commonwealth") +
    theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold"),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 14),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 12),
  )






Codecommonwealth_2020 <- commonwealth |>
  filter(year == 2020)

world <- world |>
  mutate(is_commonwealth = name %in% commonwealth_2020$country_name)

ggplot(data = world) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = is_commonwealth), color = "blue") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "red", "FALSE" = "grey90")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Commonwealth Countries in 2020", fill = "Commonwealth") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold"),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 14),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 12),
  )













Commonwealth Across Time



The number of commonwealth countries have increased between 1950 and 2020, and most of the new members come from African countries and south Asian countries. The interesting point lies in the colonial history of these countries and their relationship with the Commonwealth. Equally worthy of consideration is the relationship between this model of increasing membership in Africa and Asia and neocolonialism.

title: Paths to Democracy: Exploring Regime Transitions and Democratic Stability in the Commonwealth of Nations
text:
5.2 Democracy trends

Codecommonwealth_1950 <- commonwealth_1950 %>%
  mutate(region = case_when(
    country_name == "Australia" ~ "Oceania",
    country_name == "Canada" ~ "America",
    country_name == "India" ~ "Asia",
    country_name == "New Zealand" ~ "Oceania",
    country_name == "Pakistan" ~ "Asia",
    country_name == "South Africa" ~ "Africa",
    country_name == "Sri Lanka" ~ "Asia",
    country_name == "Tonga" ~ "Oceania",
    country_name == "United Kingdom" ~ "Europe"))

commonwealth_2020 <- commonwealth_2020 %>%
  mutate(region = case_when(
    country_name %in% c("Botswana", "Cameroon", "Ghana", "Kenya", "Lesotho", "Malawi",
                        "Mauritius", "Mozambique", "Namibia", "Nigeria", "Rwanda", 
                        "Seychelles", "Sierra Leone", "South Africa", "Swaziland", 
                        "Tanzania", "Uganda", "Zambia") ~ "Africa",
    
    country_name %in% c("Bangladesh", "Brunei", "India", "Maldives","Malaysia",
                        "Pakistan", "Singapore", "Sri Lanka") ~ "Asia",
    
    country_name %in% c("Cyprus", "Malta", "United Kingdom") ~ "Europe",
    
    country_name %in% c("Australia", "Kiribati", "Nauru", "New Zealand", 
                        "Papua New Guinea", "Samoa", "Solomon Islands", 
                        "Tonga", "Tuvalu", "Vanuatu") ~ "Oceania",
    
    country_name %in% c("Antigua and Barbuda", "Bahamas", "Barbados", "Belize", 
                        "Canada", "Dominica", "Grenada", "Guyana", "Jamaica", 
                        "St. Kitts & Nevis", "St. Lucia", "St.Vincent & Grenadines", 
                        "Trinidad &Tobago") ~ "America"))



Codeggplot(commonwealth_1950, aes(x = is_democracy, fill = region)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Democracy in Commonwealth Countries (1950)",
       x = "Democracy",
       y = "Amount of Countries",
       fill = "Region") +
  theme_minimal() 








Codeggplot(commonwealth_2020, aes(x = is_democracy, fill = region)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Democracy in Commonwealth Countries (2020)",
       x = "Democracy",
       y = "Amount of Countries",
       fill = "Region") +
  theme_minimal() 













Democracy Trends Insights



The most important takeaways from the graphed data are that overall, there was a higher trend in democratic commonwealth countries both in 1950 and 2020. However, it is important to note the increase of commonwealth countries in 2020, which makes us understand that there is a higher proportion of non-democratic countries in Africa than there were in 1950, which would be key for our further analysis.

title: Paths to Democracy: Exploring Regime Transitions and Democratic Stability in the Commonwealth of Nations
text:
5.3 Change in Regimes

Codeggplot(commonwealth_1950, aes(y = fct_infreq(regime_category), fill = region)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Regime Categories of Commonwealth Countries in 1950",
       y = "Regime Category",
       x = "Number of Countries per Regime",
       fill = "Region") +
  theme_minimal()








Codeggplot(commonwealth_2020, aes(y = fct_infreq(regime_category), fill = region)) +
  geom_bar() +
   labs(title = "Regime Categories of Commonwealth Countries in 2020",
       x = "Number of Countries per Regime",
       y = "Regime Category",
       fill = "Region") +
  theme_minimal() 













Regime Change Insights



For the next group of graphs, we decided to narrow our focus to the change in type of regime in regions of the world from 1950 to 2020. As we have seen before, there is still a higher proportion of democratic commonwealth countries, however, it is important to highlight how there is a higher amount of African commonwealth countries in 2020 that have a dictatorship regime in contrast with other regions.

title: Paths to Democracy: Exploring Regime Transitions and Democratic Stability in the Commonwealth of Nations
text:
5.4 Democrary Visualizations

Codecw_map <- world |>
  left_join(commonwealth_2020, by = c("name" = "country_name"))

ggplot(cw_map) +
   geom_sf(aes(fill = is_democracy), color = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "darkgreen", "FALSE" = "red", "NA" = "gray"),
                    labels = c("TRUE" = "Democracy", "FALSE" = "Not a Democracy", "NA" = "No Data")) +
  labs(
    title = "Current Democracy Status in Commonwealth Countries",
    fill = "Democratic State"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold"),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 14),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 12)
  )













Current Democratic States in the Commonwealth



The plot shows a world map with Commonwealth countries categorized by their current democracy status. Here’s how the countries are represented: - Green countries: These are the Commonwealth countries that are currently considered democracies. - Red countries: These are the Commonwealth countries that are not currently considered democracies.



Codelibrary(ggpattern)
library(ggthemes)

africa_map_2020 <- world |>
  filter(region_un == "Africa") |>
  left_join(commonwealth_2020, by = c("name" = "country_name"))

ggplot(africa_map_2020) +
  geom_sf_pattern(
    aes(fill = regime_category, pattern = is_democracy),
    color = "white",
    pattern_color = "white",
    pattern_density = 0.3,
    pattern_spacing = 0.02,
    pattern_key_scale_factor = 0.6,
    size = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "plasma", na.value = "gray80") +
  scale_pattern_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "stripe", "FALSE" = "none")) +
  labs(
    title = "Regime Types and Democracy Status in African Commonwealth Countries in 2020",
    fill = "Regime Type",
    pattern = "Democracy"
  ) +
  theme_map() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold"),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 14),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 12)
  )













Regime Types and Democracy Status in African Commonwealth Countries in 2020



This map highlights that African Commonwealth countries in 2020 are divided between democratic, mixed, and authoritarian systems. Southern Africa seems to be the region with relatively more stable democracies, while the central and northern regions of the continent remain significantly under authoritarian rule, with several nations still struggling with democratic transitions.

This article emphasizes the importance of effective leadership. It advises to build relationships based on trust and loyalty rather than power dynamics. Among the key practices that this article include are:

Value all ideas and encourage open expression.
Be emotionally aware and set the tone by being open and empathetic.
Resolve conflicts early and steer focus on team goals.
Communicate clearly and consistently.
Promote trust and cooperation among team members as well as between the leader and the team.
Share information and highlight how individual roles contribute to the overall mission.
Facilitate healthy communication through openness, listening, and clarification—not constant meetings.
Set clear values, goals, and performance standards, and regularly review progress.
Use consensus for decision-making, ensuring everyone is committed and heard.
Create team ground rules collaboratively and ensure everyone commits to them.

title: 3  Xi Fang
text: “” I have found an insightful article titled “Kate Spade and Co. Exec: This Is How I Pick Perfect Teammates” by Mary Beech:https://time.com/4388615/kate-spade-team-building/, Executive Vice President and Chief Marketing Officer of Kate Spade & Company. In this piece, Beech shares her experiences and principles for building effective teams, drawing from her tenure at The Walt Disney Company and Kate Spade & Company. Beech emphasizes five key principles for creating a powerful team: Passion Over Perfect Qualifications: She advocates for selecting team members who exhibit genuine passion, as it drives sustained performance and commitment. Consider the Whole Person: Beyond credentials, understanding a candidate’s interests and motivations ensures better team synergy and creativity. Diversity Over Homogeneity: Building a diverse team with complementary skills, rather than hiring in one’s likeness, fosters innovation and growth. Encourage Confidence Through ‘Plusing’: Adopting the concept of ‘plusing’—enhancing ideas collaboratively—encourages continuous improvement and confidence among team members. Active Listening: Truly paying attention to team members’ input fosters collaboration and innovation, reinforcing a culture of mutual respect.

text:
Nine essential characteristics of great teamwork
https://www.wework.com/ideas/professional-development/management-leadership/nine-characteristics-of-great-teamwork
A team’s success is highly dependent upon the participation of all its members, as the final product must showcase everyone’s work and learning. All this is subject to the team’s communication and interaction in the working process. Although there are many factors that influence this, these are some 9 essential characteristics in a team:

Great and constant communication: Typically throughout the work, this is a way to demonstrate care for each other and the project itself.
Individual Talent: Which involves the active commitment of its members to give as much as they can to the team.
Sense of Belongingness: This is important to make everyone feel welcomed in the workspace.
Strong Leadership: knowing that each member has as much saying as all of the other members.
Clear Structure: Specially in teamworks like the ones that we are doing, it is helpful to have a constant idea of what we are doing in each stage of the project.
Reachable goals: Knowing and setting what we want to achieve from the strat helps the team on balancing the amount of time and effort that they should put into each task.
Constructive Feedback: Knowing how to deliver feedback is helpful specially in avoiding misunderstandings while also demonstrating respect for eachothers work.
Positive Atitude: Even on times of stress, a positive attitude can enhance the working environment of a group by remembering that there is more beyond the working part of the project.
Focusing on solutions: In times of troubles, focusing thinking each other as a team against the deadlines is fundamental to maintain a sense of social responsibility.

title: Appendix A — Proposal
text: The rise and fall of democratic states: An exploration of democratic regimes prevalence since the mid-20th century

title: Appendix A — Proposal
text:
Team Members

Xi Fang
Pablo Jimenez Sanchez
Kirsty Herrera Garcia

title: Appendix A — Proposal
text:
Description.
This project will explore the rise and fall of democratic regimes worldwide from 1950 to 2020, analyzing the relationship between regime change and colonial ties. In the case of the rise of democracy, we will explore the indicators of democracy these states show after the regime change. In the case of the fall of democratic regimes, we will explore the type of new regimes that have proliferated.

title: Appendix A — Proposal
text:
Motivation.
In today’s global political landscape, where democratic principles face ongoing threats both domestically and internationally and authoritarian regimes have surged over the past decade, comprehending the dynamics of democratic regimes’ rise and fall is essential to effectively navigating contemporary international politics. This project aims to understand the magnitude of regime changes occurring worldwide and whether this poses a genuine threat to democratic values. We also intend to explore possible explanations for these changes and how democracy is assessed globally.

title: Appendix B — Case Study
text:
Case Study of the number of Uber drivers in NYC
In this article, by studying the number of pickups in central Manhattan traffic, they are trying to learn the relationship between the number of pickups made by Uber and the number of pickups made by taxis. This article then focuses on the details of the number of pickups that come from and tries to explain the real situation happening in the transportation market in NYC. Finally, the article explains the cause of the congestion.
The data are gathered from the Freedom of Information Law from NYC’s Taxi and Limousine Commission (TLC), which Covers Uber pickup data from April–June 2014 and April–June 2015.
From the data presented, the study highlights that Uber services have not significantly increased the risk of urban gridlock but have been replacing cabs. As we can see from the first graph, the overall pickups from both Uber and cabs increased by three million from 2014 to 2015. However, if we focus on the yellow cab pickups, we can see a decrease along with a slight increase in the green cab pickups, which explains the low overall increase.
Moreover, from the choropleth map and the point plot, there is an overall increase in Uber pickups in Manhattan and other zones that the green cabs didn’t reach before. Especially in Manhattan, the lack of cabs in this zone is underscored by the number of Uber cars that add to the surprisingly low overall pickup number. From the point plot, a negative slope demonstrates that the decrease in cab usage is proportional to the increase in Uber usage, meaning that there is an equilibrium between these services.
Lastly, although this demonstrates that cabs and users are able to coexist, the decrease in cabs and how this creates uncertainty regarding their presence is concerning.
